title: May crowning
hook: children crown a statue of Mary with flowers in May

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Miraculous Medal: a prayer stamped in metal, worn close. Your line was conceived without sin. What did you touch yesterday that reminded you? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-three.

The procession is already moving down the aisle. Children in their best clothes, some still in the white they wore for their first Communion, each holding a few flowers: tulips from a grocery store, lilacs cut from somebody's backyard, one dandelion held very seriously by a small boy. At the front stands a statue of Mary. The flowers are laid at her feet until there's a small hill of them. Then one child climbs a step, sometimes with an adult steadying the ladder, and sets a ring of flowers on the statue's head. People sing. Somebody's phone is out. And for a moment the whole parish is looking at a child's hands. Today's word is that moment.
screen: `CHILDREN, FLOWERS, A PROCESSION.` → `A HILL OF FLOWERS AT HER FEET.` → `ONE CHILD LIFTS THE CROWN.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. A May crowning is a popular devotion, not a required feast. Parishes and schools hold one in the spring, often in May, the month Catholic custom gives to Mary. Flowers for a mother, in the season of flowers. Second, why a child. In Matthew's Gospel, children in the temple are shouting hosanna, and the chief priests are annoyed. Jesus answers them with a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "Out of the mouth of infants and of sucklings thou hast perfected praise." The crowning puts that verse into practice. The grown-ups could do it more neatly. They hand it to a child anyway. Third, why flowers and not gold. Jesus points to the lilies of the field and says, "not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed as one of these." A crown of flowers is cheaper than a king's crown, and in that saying it outshines one. Catholics call Mary queen because her son is king, and the Council speaks of her exalted by the Lord as queen. But the crown a parish gives her is made of things that grow in backyards. Fourth, the line. Some readers trace the title queen of the May to old spring festivals where a girl was crowned with flowers, and a hymn sung at some crownings calls Mary queen of the angels and queen of the May in the same breath. By the end of the week, the crown will be brown and drooping, and someone will quietly take it down. That's part of it. The gift doesn't have to last to be given.
screen: `A DEVOTION, NOT A DUTY.` · `OUT OF THE MOUTH OF INFANTS.` · `NOT EVEN SOLOMON IN ALL HIS GLORY.` · `A CROWN THAT WILTS, GIVEN ANYWAY.` · then, large: `QUEEN OF THE MAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring flowers, even in your mind. Settle, and breathe. If there's a flower or a plant near you, look at it closely: one petal, one leaf, the way it's already starting to fade at an edge. If there isn't, picture the flower you would bring. Something ordinary is fine. A dandelion counts. Hold it out, in your imagination, to someone you'd like to honor. If you pray, you can offer it to Mary with the opening of the Hail Mary: Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. If you don't, simply offer the flower, and let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
May crowning. A spring devotion where a child sets a crown of flowers on a statue of Mary, and the parish sings. Today's word.
Your line: queen of the may. Today, give one small thing that won't last: a flower, a note, ten minutes of attention. Don't wait for it to be worthy. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Some Catholic parishes and schools hold a May crowning in spring: children bring flowers in procession, one child places a crown of flowers on a statue of Mary, and the people sing Marian hymns.

original.note: Latin: Queen of Angels, a title from the Litany of Loreto.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty school pageant with flowers.
what it means: a devotion where a child crowns Mary with flowers, because Catholics call her queen, and because praise from children is the praise Jesus defended.
what a scholar hears: Matthew 21:16 quoting Psalm 8, the lilies outshining Solomon, and a title some readers trace to spring festivals, taken into a devotion to Mary.

notes: Practice uses the opening of the Hail Mary in its traditional English ('Hail Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee'); its scriptural root, Luke 1:28 in the Douay-Rheims, is cited. Confirm.

Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 21:16 ('Out of the mouth of infants and of sucklings thou hast perfected praise') and Matthew 6:29 ('not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed as one of these').
'The title queen of the May was borrowed from spring festivals where a girl was crowned with flowers' is stated plainly: confirm, or soften to 'tradition says'.
The hymn described (queen of the angels, queen of the May) is 'Bring Flowers of the Rarest'; not quoted because authorship and public-domain status were not verified.
Lumen Gentium 59 paraphrased ('exalted by the Lord as queen'). Confirm.
Scene details (first Communion clothes, a ladder, a small hill of flowers) are offered as one typical crowning; customs vary by parish.
